procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Additional Civil Judge at Allahabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated the 30th July 1951 of Allahabad High Court in First Appeal No. 258 of 1943 arising out of the judgment and the decree dated the 8th March 1943 of the Court of Additional Civil Judge at Allahabad in Original Suit No. 27 of 1940.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Original Suit No. 27 of 1940 was decided by the Additional Civil Judge of Allahabad on March 8, 1943. This decision was appealed to the Allahabad High Court as First Appeal No. 258 of 1943. The Allahabad High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the Additional Civil Judge on July 30, 1951, and decreed the suit. On February 13, 1953, the High Court granted a certificate under section 110, C. P. C. and article 133 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, whose names are not explicitly mentioned in the provided text but are represented by S. K. Dar, B. S. Shastri, R. O. Ghatak and O. P. Lal, appealed to the Supreme Court from the judgment and decree of the Allahabad High Court. The High Court had reversed the decision of the Additional Civil Judge. The appeal was brought before the Supreme Court after the High Court granted a certificate under section 110, C. P. C. and article 133 of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Is the bequest made in favour of Mrs. Mistry void in law?

facts: A Parsi testator bequeathed his entire estate to Mrs. Shirinbai Mistry.
The will was attested by two witnesses, one of whom was M. B. Mistry, the husband of the beneficiary, Mrs. Mistry.
law: Section 67 of the Indian Succession Act renders a bequest void if the person to whom the bequest is made, or their spouse, attests the will.
application: The trial court applied Section 67 and found that because Mrs. Mistry's husband had attested the will, the bequest made to her was void.
The High Court agreed with the trial court's finding on this issue.
When the case was appealed to the Supreme Court, the appellant (representing Mrs. Mistry) did not question or challenge the lower courts' decisions that the bequest was void.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the concurrent findings of the lower courts that the bequest in favour of Mrs. Mistry was void under Section 67 of the Indian Succession Act. This was not a contested issue before the Supreme Court, as the appellant conceded the point and based their arguments on other grounds.

issue.issue_text: Is the defendant No. 1 the universal legatee under the will or are the other defendants, viz. Mrs.

facts: A Parsi testator bequeathed his entire estate to "Mrs. Shirinbai, her heirs, executors and administrators, for her and their own use and benefit, absolutely and for ever".
The will was attested by Mrs. Shirinbai's husband, which made the direct bequest to her void under section 67 of the Indian Succession Act.

The issue was whether the words "her heirs, executors and administrators" were merely words of limitation describing an absolute estate for Shirinbai (in which case the entire gift would fail), or if they created a separate, substitutional gift to her heirs (her daughters).
law: The central legal principle is the interpretation of a will to determine the testator's true intention.

The court must decide if the words "her heirs, executors and administrators" are used as "words of limitation" (describing the nature of the estate given) or as "words of purchase" (identifying the recipients of the gift).
Section 129 of the Indian Succession Act allows a second bequest to take effect if the first bequest fails for any reason, not just the death of the legatee.
application: The Supreme Court focused heavily on the specific phrase "for her and their own use and benefit".

The Court reasoned that if the testator's only intention was to give an absolute estate to Shirinbai, the words "her heirs, executors and administrators" followed by "absolutely and forever" would have been sufficient. The inclusion of "and their own use and benefit" was seen as a clear indication of a separate intention.
The Court stated that the provision for the "own use and benefit" of the heirs would be "wholly out of place" if they were not intended to be direct beneficiaries.

It concluded that the testator's language showed an unmistakable intention to prevent his estate from passing to his step-relations as on intestacy. To achieve this, he created a double bequest: a primary one to Shirinbai, and a successive, substitutional one to her heirs that would take effect if the first one failed.
Therefore, the words "her heirs, executors and administrators" were interpreted as words of purchase, making them independent objects of the testator's bounty.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument that the will created a substitutional bequest. It held that while the bequest to defendant No. 1 (Mrs. Shirinbai) was void, the language of the will, particularly the phrase "for her and their own use and benefit," demonstrated a clear intention to also make her heirs (her daughters, the other defendants) direct legatees. Consequently, the estate passed to them.

issue.issue_text: Whether the plaintiffs were the heirs of the deceased and were entitled to maintain the suit.

facts: The plaintiffs, who were relatives of the deceased testator, filed a suit claiming that a bequest in the will to the primary beneficiary, Shirinbai, was void.

The plaintiffs argued that because the bequest was void, the testator's estate should be treated as intestate (as if there were no will), which would make them the legal heirs entitled to the property.
The trial court found that the plaintiffs were not the testator's heirs and dismissed the suit.
The High Court reversed this, holding that the plaintiffs were indeed the heirs and were entitled to the estate.
law: Under Section 67 of the Indian Succession Act, a bequest to a person is void if their spouse attests the will. In this case, the bequest to Shirinbai was void because her husband had attested the will.
The Supreme Court considered the legal concept of a "substitutional bequest," where the will provides for an alternative beneficiary if the primary bequest fails.

The Court also considered the interpretation of the word "heirs." While technically a living person cannot have heirs, the Court noted that the term can be used in a less strict sense to mean "heirs presumptive"—the people who would be heirs if the person died at that moment.
application: The Supreme Court agreed that the primary bequest to Shirinbai failed due to Section 67.
However, the Court found that the will contained a substitutional bequest to Shirinbai's "heirs."
The Court interpreted "heirs" to mean Shirinbai's presumptive heirs at the time of the testator's death.
At that time, Shirinbai had two daughters who were her presumptive heirs.
Therefore, the Court held that this substitutional bequest to the two daughters was valid and took effect when the primary bequest to their mother failed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that because the substitutional bequest to Shirinbai's daughters was valid, the property was properly disposed of by the will and there was no intestacy. Since the plaintiffs' entire claim was based on their right to inherit upon an intestacy, they had no right to the property and therefore no standing to maintain the suit. The Court accordingly dismissed the plaintiffs' suit.

arguments.issue_text: Is the bequest made in favour of Mrs. Mistry void in law?
appellant_arguments: The provisions of section 67 of the Indian Succession Act, which would render the bequest void, were not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case.
respondent_arguments: The bequest to Mrs. Mistry (Shirinbai) is void under Section 67 of the Indian Succession Act because her husband was one of the attesting witnesses to the will.

respondent_arguments: The bequest was to Mrs. Mistry, and since it is void, the property is subject to intestacy and should be distributed among the legal heirs.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the plaintiffs were the heirs of the deceased and were entitled to maintain the suit.
appellant_arguments: The plaintiffs and proforma defendants were not the legal heirs of the testator.
The plaintiffs had no locus standi (right) to maintain the suit.
respondent_arguments: The plaintiffs are the legal heirs of the testator and are therefore entitled to file the suit and claim the estate upon intestacy.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a will makes a bequest to a person and their heirs, executors, and administrators 'for her and their own use and benefit', these words are not to be ignored. They indicate the testator's intention to create a substitutional bequest in favor of the heirs, executors, and administrators, which takes effect upon the failure of the primary bequest to the named individual.
obiter: Potential difficulties in determining the recipient of a gift if a legatee dies leaving both heirs and a will appointing an executor (who is not an heir) do not have a bearing on the construction of the testator's original intent based on the language used in the will.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the testator intended to create a primary bequest to Shirinbai for her absolute use, and upon the failure of that bequest, to make a separate, substitutional bequest to her heirs, executors, and administrators for their own absolute use and benefit, thereby preventing the property from being distributed through intestacy.
legal_tests_applied: The primary legal test applied is the ascertainment of the testator's intention through a "fair and plain reading of the will as a whole" and the specific language used.
why_appellant_lost: The provided text does not contain the court's reasoning for why the appellant lost on any issue. It only contains the reasoning for why the appellant's argument regarding the interpretation of the will was successful.
why_respondent_won: The provided text does not contain the court's reasoning for why the respondent ultimately won. Instead, it details the court's reasoning for rejecting the respondent's argument that the will created an intestacy. The court rejected this argument for the following reasons:
The phrase "for her and their own use and benefit" was interpreted as clearly indicating an intention to create a substitutional bequest for the heirs, executors, and administrators.

The court reasoned that the provision for the "'own use and benefit' of 'her heirs, executors and administrators' is only compatible with an intention of making a bequest in favour of her heirs, executors and administrators."
If the testator's intention was only to give an absolute estate to Shirinbai, the inclusion of the words "their own use and benefit" would be "wholly out of place."

The language used by the testator demonstrated a clear intention to prevent the estate from passing to his step-relations on intestacy, which he accomplished by making a provision for Shirinbai's heirs as "independent objects of a substitutional bequest."
